kurals.tamil:
அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை பிறிதின்மை
இன்மையா வையா துலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivinmai inmaiyul inmai piridhinmai
inmaiyaa vaiyaa thulagu.
kurals.meaning: Of all the kinds of lack, the lack of understanding is the real poverty; the world does not count the lack of other things, such as money, as true want.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two kids: one has an empty piggy bank but knows how to read, count and solve problems; the other has a full piggy bank but can’t figure anything out. The first one can earn coins again, but the second one will keep losing them. That is why the poet says not knowing is the emptiest pocket of all.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a paradox built on the repeated word inmai (இன்மை, lack, poverty): arivinmai (அறிவின்மை, absence of understanding) is ‘the poverty among poverties’, while piridhinmai (other lacks, chiefly of wealth) the world will not reckon as poverty at all. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render it as ‘the famine of knowledge is the cruelest famine’, and Solomon Pappaiah shifts the evaluator from ‘the world’ (ulagu) to ‘the great ones’ (periyor), reflecting the classical commentary habit of reading ulagu as ‘the wise of the world’. Puliyur Kesigan adds that material poverty is not regarded as lasting poverty, since it can be remedied, whereas folly cannot. Placed in the Natpiyal after Pedhaimai (ch. 84), Pullarivaanmai shifts the focus from simple folly to the conceited, perverse ignorance (pull-arivu, ‘petty knowledge’) of one who thinks himself wise. Text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the second line is printed in its traditional sandhi-split form ‘inmaiyaa vaiyaa thulagu’ (for vaiyaadhu ulagu).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In this world, there is nothing so sublime and pure as transcendental knowledge.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna ranks knowledge above every other purifying possession or practice.
hinduism.tie_back: If knowledge is the greatest possession, its absence is the greatest poverty, exactly Valluvar’s claim.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic inverse (value of knowledge rather than poverty of its lack); quote verified on vedabase.io.

christianity.quote_or_event: “How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs weighs wisdom against money and finds money the lesser treasure.
christianity.tie_back: Lacking gold is a small want; lacking wisdom is the real one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on the wisdom-versus-wealth comparison; verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" Only they will remember [who are] people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an poses a rhetorical question whose answer is plainly no: knowledge separates people more than anything else.
islam.tie_back: Both texts make the lack of knowledge the decisive deficiency in a person.
islam._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit; the verse ranks knowers above non-knowers but does not speak of poverty. Verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If he acquired this, what else is lacking? If he has not acquired this, what has he acquired?”
judaism.explanation: In the same passage Abaye cites a tradition that a poor person is only one lacking in intelligence, and the saying from the West follows: whoever has understanding has everything.
judaism.tie_back: Almost Valluvar’s exact thought: the only true poverty is poverty of understanding.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, including the explicit claim that the truly poor man is the one lacking intelligence; verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A worse taint than these is ignorance, the worst of all taints.”
buddhism.explanation: After listing many stains on a person’s life, the Buddha names ignorance as the deepest of them.
buddhism.tie_back: Both rank ignorance as the worst among a whole list of deficiencies.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same ‘worst of all’ ranking structure, though framed as taint rather than poverty; verified on accesstoinsight.org.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas, already rich, asks Bacchus that everything he touches turn to gold; his food and drink harden into metal and he begs to be freed from the gift, and later he earns ass’s ears for his poor judgment in the contest between Pan and Apollo.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas has endless wealth but no sense, and the wealth does him no good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Gold could not cure his real poverty, which was a poverty of judgment.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative myth rather than a teaching; fits the wealth-versus-wisdom contrast well.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius reports Socrates as saying that there is only one good, knowledge, and only one evil, ignorance.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates reduces all good and evil to the presence or absence of knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise treats the absence of knowledge as the only lack that truly matters.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 2.31
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match; paraphrased because the Hicks wording was not re-verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
அறிவிலான் நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல் பிறிதியாதும்
இல்லை பெறுவான் தவம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivilaan nenjuvandhu eedhal piridhiyaadhum
illai peruvaan thavam.
kurals.meaning: When a fool gives something away with a glad heart, the cause is nothing else but the good merit of the one who receives it.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a kid who never shares suddenly hands you his best sandwich with a big smile. You didn’t earn it from his good sense; you were just lucky that day. The poet says a fool’s gift is like that: it comes from the receiver’s good luck, not the giver’s wisdom.
kurals.university: The kural is ironic: a person without understanding (arivilaan, அறிவிலான்) does not give wisely, so if he gives nenjuvandhu (நெஞ்சுவந்து, with a gladdened heart), the explanation must lie outside him, in the thavam (தவம், austerity, accumulated merit) of the recipient (peruvaan). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss thavam as nalvinai (good karma), and the old English rendering speaks of ‘the receiver’s merit (in a former birth)’, reflecting the karmic reading of the classical commentators. Kalaignar softens it to ‘the receiver’s good fortune’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as the receiver’s own spiritual quality drawing the gift. The underlying point is that the fool’s generosity is unreliable and unearned, an accident of providence rather than a virtue. No textual variants appear between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And charity performed at an impure place, at an improper time, to unworthy persons, or without proper attention and respect is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classifies giving by the understanding behind it, and gift without discernment belongs to tamas, the mode of ignorance.
hinduism.tie_back: A fool’s gift has no wisdom behind it; any good it does is not the giver’s doing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of ignorant giving but not the kural’s point about the receiver’s merit; verified on vedabase.io.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And it shall be, that thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there.”
christianity.explanation: God feeds Elijah through ravens, creatures that give without any understanding of what they do.
christianity.tie_back: The gift reaches the receiver because of who he is before God, not because of the giver’s wisdom.
christianity._accuracy_note: Loose analogical match (providential gift through an unknowing agent); verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision, and He knows its place of dwelling and place of storage.”
islam.explanation: Provision (rizq) is assigned by God; whoever hands it over is only the channel.
islam.tie_back: As in the kural, what the receiver gets is due to what was allotted to him, not the giver’s sense.
islam._accuracy_note: Theological parallel on allotted provision; does not mention fools. Verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the Book of Esther, the fickle King Ahasuerus, who earlier approved Haman’s decree, is moved after a sleepless night to heap honor on Mordecai and later grants Esther’s plea.
judaism.explanation: Jewish tradition reads the turn of events as hidden providence working through an unreliable ruler.
judaism.tie_back: The king’s generosity came not from his wisdom but from the merit and destiny of those who received it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Interpretive analogy; Esther does not state this moral explicitly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta the Buddha describes four kinds of purification of an offering, including one purified by the recipient but not by the giver: the giver lacks virtue, yet the gift bears fruit because the recipient is virtuous.
buddhism.explanation: The worth of a gift can come entirely from the person who receives it.
buddhism.tie_back: Very close to Valluvar: a gift from an unworthy giver yields good because of the receiver’s merit.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (merit located in the recipient); paraphrased, not quoted.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ comedy Plutus, the god of wealth is blind, which is why riches fall to people at random rather than to the deserving.
greek_mythology.explanation: Wealth flows without discernment; who gets it is not decided by anyone’s wisdom.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fool’s gift is similarly blind; its landing on someone reflects their luck.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose fit: shares the theme of undiscerning giving, but credits chance rather than merit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the generous person gives to the right people, the right amounts and at the right time, whereas the prodigal gives without discrimination, often to those who should not receive.
philosophy.explanation: Real generosity needs practical wisdom; giving without it is not a virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise refuses to credit the fool’s gift as virtue; any benefit is the receiver’s good fortune.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the link between wisdom and right giving but not the receiver’s-merit claim.

kurals.tamil:
அறிவிலார் தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை
செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivilaar thaandhammaip peezhikkum peezhai
seruvaarkkum seydhal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: The suffering fools bring upon themselves is greater than anything even their enemies could manage to inflict on them.
kurals.elementary: Think of a kid who won’t wear a coat in the snow, eats all the candy at once and then skips homework. No bully could make his day as miserable as he has made it himself. The poet says fools are their own worst enemies.
kurals.university: Valluvar uses the doubled noun-verb peezhikkum peezhai (பீழிக்கும் பீழை, the affliction with which they afflict) to stress self-made misery, and seruvaar (செறுவார், those who hate, enemies) to set up the comparison. All the modern commentators agree on the sense: the harm fools do to themselves exceeds what an enemy could achieve (Mu. Varadarasanar: ‘of a measure even their foes cannot inflict’; Kalaignar: ‘the torment enemies could not deliver, fools give themselves’). Puliyur Kesigan notes the distress-causing nature (varuththam) of such self-inflicted suffering. The thought links this chapter to the Natpiyal’s concern with enemies: for the fool, the most dangerous enemy is internal. Both web texts read identically.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For him who has conquered the mind, the mind is the best of friends; but for one who has failed to do so, his mind will remain the greatest enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that an uncontrolled mind becomes a person’s worst adversary.
hinduism.tie_back: The fool’s own mind does him more harm than any outside enemy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on self as greatest enemy; verified on vedabase.io.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A fool’s mouth is his destruction, and his lips are the snare of his soul.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs shows the fool trapping himself with his own words.
christianity.tie_back: The fool’s ruin comes from inside, not from his enemies.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on self-destruction, focused on speech; verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but it is the people who are wronging themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an places the source of human ruin in people’s own choices.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, it says the deepest harm is self-inflicted.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on self-wronging; verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Fools fold their hands together / And have to eat their own flesh.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet pictures the idle fool as devouring himself.
judaism.tie_back: A vivid image of the self-inflicted affliction Valluvar describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong image of self-harm through folly (specifically idleness); verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever harm an enemy may do to an enemy, or a hater to a hater, an ill-directed mind inflicts on oneself a greater harm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares enemy harm with self-harm and finds the latter greater.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the same comparison the kural makes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, including the enemy comparison; verified on accesstoinsight.org.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon cuts down Ceres’ sacred oak despite warnings, is cursed with insatiable hunger, sells everything he owns and finally begins to devour his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: His own reckless choice becomes a hunger that destroys him from within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: No enemy could have ruined him as thoroughly as his own folly did.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative myth; the punishment is divine, but the cause is his own impious folly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that people are disturbed not by things but by their judgments about things, and that the uninstructed blame others for their troubles while the instructed look to themselves.
philosophy.explanation: Our suffering is largely produced by our own faulty judgments.
philosophy.tie_back: The fool’s self-made pain matches the Stoic diagnosis of self-caused distress.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the Stoic focus is on judgment rather than folly as such.

kurals.tamil:
வெண்மை எனப்படுவ தியாதெனின் ஒண்மை
உடையம்யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Venmai enappaduva dhiyaadhenin onmai
udaiyamyaam ennum serukku.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what stupidity is, it is the arrogance that says, “We are the wise ones.”
kurals.elementary: A kid who says “I already know everything, I don’t need to listen” stops learning right there. The poet says that feeling of being sure you are the smartest is exactly what being foolish means.
kurals.university: The kural defines folly by a pair of light-words: venmai (வெண்மை, literally ‘whiteness’, i.e. blankness, emptiness of mind) is set against onmai (ஒண்மை, ‘brightness’, i.e. keen intelligence). Folly is not mere blankness but the serukku (செருக்கு, conceit, intoxicated pride) that claims brightness: ‘udaiyam yaam’, ‘we possess it’, with the royal or self-inflating plural. Mu. Varadarasanar equates venmai with pullarivu, the chapter’s key term; Pappaiah calls it a ‘delusion’ (mayakkam) and Kalaignar ‘arrogance’ (aanavam). Structurally the kural mirrors 831 in the preceding chapter (‘pedhaimai enbadhondru yaadhenin…’), giving a definition in question-and-answer form. Text identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Fools dwelling in darkness, wise in their own conceit, and puffed up with vain knowledge, go round and round, staggering to and fro, like blind men led by the blind.”
hinduism.explanation: Yama describes those who think themselves learned while remaining in ignorance.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Wise in their own conceit’ is precisely Valluvar’s definition of folly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on conceit of wisdom; verified on sacred-texts.com.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs ranks the self-satisfied ‘wise man’ below even the plain fool.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts locate the worst folly in thinking oneself wise.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “[They are] those whose effort is lost in worldly life, while they think that they are doing well in work.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people who are confidently wrong about the worth of their own deeds.
islam.tie_back: Their false certainty is the same conceit the kural names as folly.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on self-deceived confidence, applied to deeds rather than wisdom; verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ah, / Those who are so wise— / In their own opinion; / So clever— / In their own judgment!”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah pronounces woe on those whose wisdom exists only in their own eyes.
judaism.tie_back: Self-assessed brilliance is exactly the serukku Valluvar condemns.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match; verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least to that extent, but a fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that self-awareness redeems a fool, but the conceit of wisdom seals his folly.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same definition: real folly is believing oneself wise.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; verified on accesstoinsight.org.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Arachne, a gifted weaver, boasts that her skill surpasses Minerva’s and refuses the goddess’s warning to be humble; she loses the contest of pride and is turned into a spider.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her downfall comes from overrating herself and dismissing counsel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The pride that says ‘we are the wise ones’ is the folly Valluvar defines.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Arachne is genuinely skilled, so the match is to pride rather than to empty conceit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates finds that his only advantage over a reputed wise man is that he does not mistake ignorance for knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: The kural’s folly is the reputed wise man’s condition: claiming a wisdom he lacks.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; verified on classics.mit.edu.

kurals.tamil:
கல்லாத மேற்கொண் டொழுகல் கசடற
வல்லதூஉம் ஐயம் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallaadha merkon dozhugal kasadara
valladhooum aiyam tharum.
kurals.meaning: Pretending to know what you never learned makes people doubt even the things you have truly mastered.
kurals.elementary: If a boy who is great at football starts bragging that he is also a chess champion, and everyone sees he can’t play chess, they start wondering whether he is really good at football either. Faking one thing makes people doubt the real things too.
kurals.university: Kallaadha (கல்லாத, what one has not learned) set against kasadara valladhu (கசடற வல்லது, what one has mastered without flaw) gives the kural its hinge, and the emphatic -ooum (‘even that’) shows the reach of the damage: aiyam (ஐயம், doubt) spreads from the pretended to the genuine. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read kallaadha as unread books (nool), so the fool pretends to scholarship; Kalaignar widens it to any field one pretends to know. Puliyur Kesigan reads merkondu ozhugal more actively as rashly undertaking a task one has not learned, which casts doubt even on work one could do perfectly. The kural is a pointed observation about credibility: a single exposed pretense devalues an entire reputation. Both sources give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra a jackal who falls into a vat of indigo dye passes himself off as a new king of the beasts; when he hears other jackals howl and howls back, his true nature is exposed and he loses everything.
hinduism.explanation: The fable mocks the impostor whose pretense is found out by a single slip.
hinduism.tie_back: Once the pretense is exposed, nothing he claimed is believed any more.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good illustrative fit on exposed pretense; the jackal has no genuine skill to lose credit for.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes would-be teachers who claim expertise they do not have.
christianity.tie_back: This is the posture Valluvar warns against: acting learned in what one has not learned.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the pretense, not the loss of credibility; verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids claiming or acting on what one does not know.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar gives the worldly cost of the same fault: lost trust.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit on not overreaching one’s knowledge; verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And concerning that which he has not heard, he says: I have not heard; And he acknowledges the truth.”
judaism.explanation: Among the seven marks of the wise person, the Mishnah lists honestly admitting what one has not learned.
judaism.tie_back: The wise admit gaps; the fool pretends and so loses credit for what he does know.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct positive counterpart to the kural; verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sihacamma Jataka a merchant’s donkey, dressed in a lion’s skin, is left to graze in fields; villagers fear it until it brays, revealing itself, and it is beaten.
buddhism.explanation: The borrowed image of strength collapses the moment the true voice is heard.
buddhism.tie_back: Pretended mastery, once exposed, brings disgrace instead of respect.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Classic tale of exposed pretense; paraphrased, and does not address genuine skill being doubted.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon insists on driving his father Helios’ sun chariot though he has never learned how; he loses control, scorches the earth and is struck down.
greek_mythology.explanation: He takes up a task he has not mastered, with disastrous results.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Undertaking what one has not learned, as Puliyur Kesigan reads the kural, brings ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Matches rash undertaking, not the credibility point.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters, and this defect in them overshadowed their wisdom.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates found that skilled craftsmen spoiled their real expertise by claiming knowledge beyond it.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the kural: pretending to unlearned knowledge clouds even real mastery.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on overreach eclipsing genuine skill; verified on classics.mit.edu.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றம் மறைத்தலோ புல்லறிவு தம்வயின்
குற்றம் மறையா வழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Atram maraiththalo pullarivu thamvayin
kutram maraiyaa vazhi.
kurals.meaning: If you do not get rid of your faults, then carefully covering your body with clothes is itself foolishness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who irons a perfect shirt every morning but is mean to everyone all day. Looking neat on the outside doesn’t hide the meanness. The poet says hiding your body but not fixing your faults is silly.
kurals.university: Atram (அற்றம்) here means the parts of the body to be covered, nakedness; maraiththal is covering it. Valluvar sets this against kutram (குற்றம், fault, moral defect) that remains unhidden (maraiyaa), arguing that modesty about the body while one’s faults stay on display is pullarivu, the very ‘petty understanding’ the chapter is named for. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all take ‘covering faults’ to mean removing them (neekkuthal), not concealing them, and Puliyur Kesigan adds the image of the hypocrite fully clothed and walking about ‘as though good’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads atram differently, as ‘ruin’ or ‘loss’, giving a minority interpretation that concealing one’s downfall is the petty act. Text identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains the senses of action but whose mind dwells on sense objects certainly deludes himself and is called a pretender.”
hinduism.explanation: Outward restraint without inner change is called self-deception.
hinduism.tie_back: Like clothing the body while keeping one’s faults, it is surface without substance.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the outer-versus-inner theme; not about clothing or faults specifically. Verified on vedabase.io.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus condemns those who keep the outside polished while the inside stays corrupt.
christianity.tie_back: The kural’s well-dressed fool with uncorrected faults is a whited sepulchre.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on outward cover versus inner fault; verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “O children of Adam, We have bestowed upon you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment. But the clothing of righteousness - that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names bodily clothing and then points to righteousness as the better covering.
islam.tie_back: Almost Valluvar’s exact contrast: covering nakedness matters less than covering oneself with virtue.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match (clothing for nakedness versus the garment of righteousness); verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: After eating from the forbidden tree, Adam and Eve sew fig leaves to cover their nakedness and hide among the trees, then each shifts the blame for the wrongdoing to another.
judaism.explanation: Their first instinct is to cover the body and hide, not to admit and set right the fault.
judaism.tie_back: They hide nakedness while leaving the real fault uncorrected, the folly the kural names.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel; the Torah does not draw the kural’s moral explicitly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope’s hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha mocks the ascetic whose outward dress is perfect while his mind stays tangled.
buddhism.tie_back: Same folly: tending the outer covering and leaving the inner fault.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match, including the garment image and the word ‘witless’; verified on accesstoinsight.org.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon tells of the shepherd Gyges, whose ring makes him invisible and who then commits injustice freely, to argue that people value seeming just more than being just.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth separates outward reputation from inner character.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The kural rejects caring for appearances while the fault underneath is untouched.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose fit: about appearance versus reality of justice, not about clothing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At the close of the Phaedrus, Socrates prays to Pan to be made beautiful in the inner man and that his outward and inward selves be at one.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates asks for inner beauty first and outer agreement with it.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise demands that the inner person be set right, not just the outer covering.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; good thematic parallel on inner versus outer.

kurals.tamil:
அருமறை சோரும் அறிவிலான் செய்யும்
பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Arumarai sorum arivilaan seyyum
perumirai thaane thanakku.
kurals.meaning: The fool who lets precious counsel slip, whether by ignoring good advice or by failing to guard a vital secret, does great harm to himself.
kurals.elementary: If your coach gives you a secret play and you shout it across the field, or you just forget it because you weren’t listening, your own team loses. The poet says the fool who lets good advice slip away hurts himself most.
kurals.university: The crux is arumarai sorum (அருமறை சோரும்): arumarai is ‘a rare/precious marai’, where marai may mean a secret, a hidden counsel, or a sacred teaching, and sorum means ‘lets slip, lets go loose’. Mu. Varadarasanar follows the traditional reading: the fool fails to keep a precious secret in his mind and blurts it out. Pappaiah and Kalaignar instead read it as failing to accept or follow precious advice, Puliyur Kesigan as studying the rare scriptures yet growing slack and missing their true sense, and Sivayogi Sivakumar as abandoning rare insights. All converge on the second line: perumirai (பெருமிறை, great harm or affliction) is done by the fool thaane thanakku, ‘himself to himself’, echoing 843. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Udyoga Parva, Duryodhana repeatedly rejects the counsel of Vidura, Bhishma, Drona and finally Krishna himself to make peace with the Pandavas, and the war that follows destroys him and his house.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata presents Duryodhana as the archetype of the ruler who throws away wise advice.
hinduism.tie_back: Letting precious counsel slip brought on him a ruin no enemy could have engineered alone.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match for the advice-rejecting reading; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “They would none of my counsel: they despised all my reproof. Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices.”
christianity.explanation: Wisdom warns that those who refuse counsel will reap the results of their own choices.
christianity.tie_back: The harm falls on the fool himself, just as the kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on rejected counsel bringing self-harm; verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they will say, "If only we had been listening or reasoning, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze."”
islam.explanation: The damned confess that their ruin came from failing to listen and reflect.
islam.tie_back: Their great harm was self-made by letting the warning slip.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on ignored counsel causing self-ruin; verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Rehoboam rejects the counsel of the elders who served his father Solomon to lighten the people’s burden and follows his young companions instead; the ten northern tribes break away from him.
judaism.explanation: The narrative shows a ruler losing most of his kingdom by discarding wise advice.
judaism.tie_back: Rehoboam’s loss was the perumirai he did to himself by letting good counsel go.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a wise adviser to a guide to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool lets that precious ‘hidden’ counsel slip, losing the treasure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Positive counterpart; the ‘hidden treasure’ image nicely echoes arumarai. Verified on accesstoinsight.org.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus warns his son Icarus to fly a middle course, neither too low nor too near the sun; Icarus ignores the advice, the wax melts and he falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: Clear instructions are given and thrown away in a moment of thrill.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Icarus’ fall is harm done by himself to himself through neglected counsel.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustrative match on ignored advice and self-ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If any man is able to convince me and show me that I do not think or act right, I will gladly change; for I seek the truth by which no man was ever injured. But he is injured who abides in his error and ignorance.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus welcomes correction and notes that the person who refuses it harms himself.
philosophy.tie_back: The one who rejects counsel and stays in error is injured by his own hand, as the kural says.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match including the self-injury point; verified on classics.mit.edu.

kurals.tamil:
ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான்தேறான் அவ்வுயிர்
போஒம் அளவுமோர் நோய்.
kurals.transliteration:
Evavum seygalaan thaandheraan avvuyir
poom alavumor noi.
kurals.meaning: Someone who will not do what is right even when told, and cannot figure it out for himself, is like a disease that lasts until the day he dies.
kurals.elementary: Some kids can figure out on their own to pack their bag; others at least do it when Mum reminds them. But a kid who won’t think of it and won’t listen when told stays stuck forever. The poet says that kind of stubbornness is like a sickness that never goes away.
kurals.university: Valluvar names two routes to right action, being told (evavum, ஏவவும், ‘even when commanded’) and working it out oneself (thaan theral, தான் தேறல், self-ascertainment), and condemns the person who has neither. Such a life is ‘or noi’ (ஓர் நோய், a disease) until the soul departs (poom, the poetic lengthened form of pogum, marked by the alapedai -oom). Commentators differ on whose disease: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar make it a lifelong affliction for the person himself, while Pappaiah, like the classical gloss reflected in the English ‘a burden (to the earth)’, makes him a disease to the world. Kalaignar’s idiom ‘neither sondha-puththi nor sol-puththi’ (neither one’s own wit nor heeding others’ words) neatly captures the double failure. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But ignorant and faithless persons who doubt the revealed scriptures do not attain God consciousness; they fall down. For the doubting soul there is happiness neither in this world nor in the next.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a person who neither knows nor trusts the teaching given to him.
hinduism.tie_back: Having neither insight nor willingness to be taught leaves a person without relief, a lifelong affliction.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘neither knows nor accepts teaching’ structure; religious rather than practical framing. Verified on vedabase.io.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that someone who keeps rejecting correction ends beyond cure.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Without remedy’ echoes the incurable lifelong noi of the kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on refusing correction; lacks the ‘can’t learn on his own’ half. Verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “Deaf, dumb and blind - so they will not return [to the right path].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people closed to guidance from every direction.
islam.tie_back: Neither hearing advice nor seeing for themselves, they remain stuck, as in the kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Thematic parallel about imperviousness to guidance; context concerns hypocrites. Verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is wise? He who learns from every man.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma defines wisdom as the readiness to learn from anyone.
judaism.tie_back: The kural’s fool is the exact opposite: he learns from no one and cannot teach himself.
judaism._accuracy_note: Inverse parallel rather than a direct statement about the fool; verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: Even lifelong contact with a teacher does not help someone who cannot take in what is offered.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘All his life’ matches the kural’s ‘until the soul departs’: the fool stays unchanged to the end.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on lifelong unteachability; verified on accesstoinsight.org.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus warns his brother Epimetheus never to accept a gift from Zeus; Epimetheus, whose name means ‘afterthought’, accepts Pandora anyway and understands his mistake only after the harm is done.
greek_mythology.explanation: Epimetheus neither foresees danger himself nor heeds the warning he was given.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the kural’s double failure: no insight of his own and no obedience to counsel.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close mythic embodiment of the double failure; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle quotes Hesiod: the best man thinks things through himself, the next best listens to one who advises well, but the man who neither understands for himself nor takes to heart what another says is useless.
philosophy.explanation: This three-tier ranking of people by how they come to know what to do is a classic in Greek ethics.
philosophy.tie_back: The kural describes exactly the third, worthless tier, adding that it lasts a lifetime.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.4, quoting Hesiod, Works and Days 293–297
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one structural match; paraphrased because the translation wording was not re-verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான் காணாதான்
கண்டானாம் தான்கண்ட வாறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaanaadhaan kaattuvaan thaankaanaan kaanaadhaan
kandaanaam thaankanda vaaru.
kurals.meaning: Whoever tries to show the truth to a fool ends up looking like the fool himself, because the fool is sure he already sees everything in his own way.
kurals.elementary: Try explaining to a little brother who is sure the moon follows his car that it only looks that way. He just laughs at you and says you don’t understand. The poet says that when you try to teach someone who is sure he’s right, you end up looking silly.
kurals.university: The kural is a wordplay on kaan (காண், to see): kaanaadhaan (one who does not see) is set against kaattuvaan (one who shows) and kandaan (one who has seen), and the line turns on ‘thaankanda vaaru’ (in the way he himself saw). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: one who tries to enlighten a fool becomes a fool himself, while the fool appears wise by his own lights; Pappaiah adds that the fool regards his teacher as the fool. Kalaignar sharpens the second half: the fool shows himself off as wise on the strength of what he alone knows. Puliyur Kesigan gives a different construal: the fool who shows others only what he saw remains one who never saw the truth. The density of the kaan-roots makes the kural famous for its sound-play. Both sources give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And that knowledge by which one is attached to one kind of work as the all in all, without knowledge of the truth, and which is very meager, is said to be in the mode of darkness.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita defines the lowest knowledge as a narrow view mistaken for the whole.
hinduism.tie_back: The fool ‘sees as he has seen’ and takes his small view for everything.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on partial knowledge taken as total; lacks the teacher-made-a-fool half. Verified on vedabase.io.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs advises against trying to teach a fool, who will only scorn the teaching.
christianity.tie_back: The kural’s would-be teacher is scorned and made to look the fool.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match; verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “Take what is given freely, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to urge what is right but not to get entangled with the obstinately ignorant.
islam.tie_back: Arguing with the fool only makes the teacher look foolish, so wisdom turns away.
islam._accuracy_note: Practical advice consistent with the kural, not an explicit statement of its paradox. Verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs warns that whoever corrects a scoffer brings shame on himself, and advises not to rebuke a scoffer lest he hate you, but to rebuke a wise man who will love you for it.
judaism.explanation: Instruction helps only those willing to receive it; aimed at the scoffer, it rebounds on the teacher.
judaism.tie_back: This is the kural’s first half: the teacher of the fool is the one who ends up disgraced.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match; paraphrased because the JPS wording could not be fetched this session.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Udana, a king has blind men touch different parts of an elephant; each declares the elephant is like a pot, a fan, a pillar or a brush according to the part he felt, and they come to blows over it.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the parable for teachers who cling to partial views and quarrel over them.
buddhism.tie_back: Each blind man ‘sees as he has seen’ and cannot be taught otherwise, exactly kandaanaam thaankanda vaaru.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on self-certain partial seeing; paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra, given true prophecy but cursed by Apollo never to be believed, foresees the fall of Troy and Agamemnon’s murder, yet those around her dismiss her as raving.
greek_mythology.explanation: The one who truly sees is taken for mad by those who cannot see.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the kural’s teacher, the seer is made to look the fool by the unseeing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit on the truth-teller being taken for the fool; the cause is a divine curse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the allegory of the cave, the prisoner who has seen the sun returns to free the others; with eyes unused to the dark he seems ridiculous to them, and they would rather kill him than be led up.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows the cave-dwellers mocking the one who tries to show them reality.
philosophy.tie_back: The teacher looks the fool, while the prisoners trust what they themselves have seen.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match to both halves of the kural; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான் வையத்து
அலகையா வைக்கப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulagaththaar undenbadhu illenbaan vaiyaththu
alagaiyaa vaikkap padum.
kurals.meaning: Whoever flatly denies what the wise of the world affirm to be true will be regarded on this earth as a demon and kept apart.
kurals.elementary: If everyone has seen the sun rise every morning and one boy keeps insisting “There is no sun!”, people stop taking him seriously and leave him out of games. The poet says that someone who denies what everyone knows is true gets treated like a spooky outsider.
kurals.university: Ulagaththaar (உலகத்தார்) here, as often in the Kural, means not the crowd but the learned of the world (Pappaiah: ‘the great ones’, uyarndhor), and their ‘undu’ (it exists) is denied by the fool’s ‘il’ (it does not). The traditional commentators gloss what is denied as established truths such as the other world, merit and the divine, attested by the learned; Kalaignar gives a modern secular reading: denying what has been clearly shown with evidence. Such a person is placed (vaikkappadum) as an alagai (அலகை, a demon, ghost or pey) on earth, that is, shunned as something not quite human. Sivayogi Sivakumar and Mu. Varadarasanar both stress exclusion (oduhukkappaduvaan, vilakkappaduvaan). The chapter thus ends with perverse denial as the extreme of pullarivu. Text identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They say that this world is unreal, with no foundation, no God in control. They say it is produced of sex desire and has no cause other than lust.”
hinduism.explanation: In the chapter on divine and demoniac natures, Krishna lists the denial of the world’s divine order as a mark of the asuric (demonic) person.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise brands the denier of what the wise affirm as an alagai, a demon on earth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Striking match including the ‘demonic’ label; verified on vedabase.io.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools,”
christianity.explanation: Paul says those who refuse to acknowledge what is plainly evident in creation became fools while claiming wisdom.
christianity.tie_back: Denial of what is evident marks the fool, as in the kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Fits the folly of denial; the ‘demon’ outcome is absent. Verified against bible-api KJV.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they rejected them, while their [inner] selves were convinced thereof, out of injustice and haughtiness. So see how was the end of the corrupters.”
islam.explanation: Pharaoh’s people deny Moses’ clear signs out of arrogance, though inwardly convinced.
islam.tie_back: This is the perverse denial of evident truth Kalaignar reads into the kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on willful denial of the evident; verified via alquran.cloud.

judaism.explanation: The Psalm’s naval (often rendered ‘fool’) says in his heart what the JPS note gives literally as ‘There is no God’.
judaism.tie_back: The denier of what the world affirms is the Psalmist’s naval, a morally corrupt fool.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; the RJPS renders naval as ‘scoundrel’ and notes the literal ‘There is no God’. Verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Payasi Sutta, Prince Payasi insists there is no other world, no spontaneously reborn beings and no fruit of good or bad deeds, and the monk Kumara Kassapa answers him with a long series of parables until he relents.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta treats denial of the other world and of karmic results as a wrong view to be patiently corrected.
buddhism.tie_back: Payasi denies exactly what the traditional commentators say the kural’s fool denies.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in content of denial; unlike the kural, Payasi is reasoned with rather than shunned.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Pentheus of Thebes refuses to accept the divinity of Dionysus that the women and elders of the city acknowledge, imprisons the god in disguise, and is torn apart by the maenads.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides presents Pentheus’ obstinate denial as a fatal madness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The man who denies what all around him affirm ends as an outcast and horror.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematic parallel on denial and destruction; the kural’s outcome is social exclusion, not death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle holds that what everyone believes is so, and that someone who attacks this common belief will hardly have anything more credible to put in its place.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, shared reputable opinion (endoxa) carries real evidential weight.
philosophy.tie_back: The kural likewise treats flat denial of what the world affirms as a mark of folly.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close philosophical parallel; paraphrased because the Ross wording was not re-verified this session.
